findings.chapter: Chapter 5 — From Workload to Model Selection
findings.evidence: "The ~50 tok/s here (this worked example’s low-batch decode point, ~20 ms/token — the canonical batch-1 rate at 25 ms/token is ~40 tok/s, Ch 2) and Chapter 15’s prefill-side rate are therefore different phases of the same host, not two values for one quantity. The per-dollar figures therefore scale up substantially at batch, and the 9,000 tokens-per-dollar figure should be read as a floor set by the single-stream assumption, not as the host’s economic optimum."
findings.issue: The prose correctly distinguishes the illustrative 50 tok/s single-stream point from the canonical 40 tok/s batch-1 budget point and from Chapter 15’s batched serving rate. However, the same paragraph earlier says "the same host’s per-GPU shard batch-1 weight-read floor is only ~5.2 ms/token ... so a ~20 ms single-stream step needs no batching." That sentence can be read as implying a 50 tok/s single-stream rate is supported by the weight-read floor alone, which the text then explicitly denies. The local contrast is present but easy to misread because the 5.2 ms floor and the 20 ms illustrative step are separated from the denial.
findings.fix_instruction: Tighten the sentence to say: "The ~5.2 ms weight-read floor is not a single-stream latency prediction; it only shows that weight streaming alone would not force a ~20 ms step. The 50 tok/s rate remains an illustrative chosen point, not a rate derived from that floor."

findings.evidence: Page 109, Table 5-1 footnote: "the model-to-model ratio equals the parameter ratio (bge-large ≈ 3× mpnet)". Check: bge-large = ~335M params, mpnet = ~110M params; 335/110 = 3.05 ≈ 3× ✓. Then: "the proxy overstates each model's compute most for the smallest, and the proxy ratio (4.8×) is a lower bound on the true body-only compute ratio (≈7.7×), not an upper bound." Check: MiniLM = ~23M, mpnet = ~110M; 110/23 = 4.78 ≈ 4.8× ✓. Body-only: mpnet body = 86.6M, MiniLM body = 11.3M; 86.6/11.3 = 7.66 ≈ 7.7× ✓. And 4.8 < 7.7 so 4.8 is indeed a lower bound on 7.7 ✓. All arithmetic correct.
findings.issue: No arithmetic defect — embedding model ratios and body-only derivations recompute correctly.

findings.evidence: Page 117, Figure 5.1: The caption says "the system decision the figure outputs is provisional: it is conditional on lying below Q* (§5.3(c)), and Q* is unmeasured for this workload". Cross-checking §5.3(c) on p.111: "Below Q*, RAG + guardrails is economically dominant... Above it, fine-tuning may recover its upfront cost". The figure's claim that the decision is "conditional on lying below Q*" correctly mirrors §5.3(c)'s logic ✓. Also the figure says "[ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]" for provenance — appropriate for a conceptual figure ✓.
findings.issue: No defect — Figure 5.1's caption accurately reflects the text in §5.3(c) regarding the conditional nature of the decision.

findings.evidence: Page 107, Table 5-2: "Total tokens per dollar (single-stream decode + overlapped prefill; not the 10 rps fleet point): ~285,000 tokens per dollar at 300 output tokens/request — 50 × (1 + 9,200/300) ≈ 1,583 tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20". Check: 9200/300 = 30.667; 1 + 30.667 = 31.667; 50 × 31.667 = 1,583.3 ✓; 1583 × 3600/20 = 1583 × 180 = 284,940 ≈ 285,000 ✓. Also "Total tokens per dollar (serial single-stream floor, no overlap; 20 ms/token basis): ~242,000 tokens per dollar — 9,500/7.08 ≈ 1,342 tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20; 7.08 s = 1.08 s prefill + 6.0 s decode at the illustrative 20 ms/token rate". Check: 300 × 0.020 = 6.0 s ✓; 1.08 + 6.0 = 7.08 s ✓; 9500/7.08 = 1,341.8 ≈ 1,342 ✓; 1342 × 180 = 241,560 ≈ 242,000 ✓. Also "~199,000 tokens per dollar — 9,500/8.58 ≈ 1,107 tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20; 8.58 s = 1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode at the canonical 25 ms/token rate". Check: 300 × 0.025 = 7.5 ✓; 1.08 + 7.5 = 8.58 ✓; 9500/8.58 = 1,107.2 ≈ 1,107 ✓; 1107 × 180 = 199,260 ≈ 199,000 ✓. All correct.
findings.issue: No arithmetic defect — all three per-dollar token figures in Table 5-2 recompute correctly.

findings.evidence: Page 109, Economics unit note: "Ch 4's ~2.76M input tokens per dollar divides the whole fleet's ~92,000 input tok/s by the fleet's ~$120/hr spend at ~6 hosts — ~15,300 input tok/s per host at the same ~$20/hr per-host price". Check: 92000/6 = 15,333 ≈ 15,300 ✓. "this chapter's ~285,000 divides one host's 1,583 tok/s combined single-stream rate by that same ~$20/hr". Check: 1583/20 × 3600 = 1583 × 180 = 284,940 ≈ 285,000 ✓. "The denominators are per-host on both sides, so the ~10× gap between the two figures is the single-stream-to-batched (occupancy) factor". Check: 2.76M/285K = 9.68 ≈ 10× ✓. Consistent.
findings.issue: No arithmetic defect — cross-chapter per-dollar reconciliation correctly computes the ~10× gap as occupancy factor.

findings.evidence: Page 105, §5.3(a): "index storage for a D-dim float32 vector corpus is bytes = nchunks × D × 4 ... For 768-dim: 1×10⁶ × 768 × 4 = 3.07 GB; for 384-dim: 1×10⁶ × 384 × 4 = 1.54 GB; a difference of ~1.5 GB." Check: 10⁶ × 768 × 4 = 3,072,000,000 B = 3.07 GB ✓; 10⁶ × 384 × 4 = 1,536,000,000 B = 1.54 GB ✓; difference = 3.07 − 1.54 = 1.53 ≈ 1.5 GB ✓. "At 10× the corpus (10 M chunks), that difference grows to ~15 GB" — check: 10 × 1.53 = 15.3 ≈ 15 GB ✓. All correct.
findings.issue: No arithmetic defect — index storage calculations recompute correctly.

findings.evidence: Page 105, §5.3(a): "~186–371 ms if encoded on a single CPU core at ~30–60 GFLOP/s sustained (~200 GFLOP/s is the AVX-512 theoretical peak, not a sustained rate), but only ~1.1 ms on a ~10 TFLOP/s GPU". Check CPU: 11.14 GFLOP / 30 GFLOP/s = 0.371 s = 371 ms; 11.14/60 = 0.186 s = 186 ms ✓. Check GPU: 11.14/10,000 = 0.001114 s ≈ 1.1 ms ✓. Also states "single-core encoding would require ≈92.8 GFLOP/s sustained per core (11.14 GFLOP ÷ 0.12 s)". Check: 11.14/0.12 = 92.83 ≈ 92.8 ✓. All correct.
findings.issue: No arithmetic defect — embedding compute timing figures recompute correctly across CPU and GPU.

findings.evidence: Page 111, §5.3(c): The Q* formula is stated as "Q* = (Ctrain + Cweights-extra) / (ΔQ · value per corrected query)" with the note that it "omits the recurring per-query prefill/retrieval saving that fine-tuning's shorter context would confer, so it yields an upper bound on the true break-even volume — a conservative (higher) estimate". This is logically sound: omitting a benefit of the numerator-side alternative (fine-tuning's recurring savings) means you need MORE queries to break even, making Q* an upper bound. The note correctly identifies the direction of the bias ✓.
findings.issue: No defect — the Q* formula's upper-bound characterization and its omitted-term analysis are logically correct.

findings.evidence: Page 130: "Output tokens per dollar (single-stream decode, 50 tok/s) | 9,000 output tokens per dollar | 50 tok/s × 3600 s/hr ÷ $20/hr [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]" and "Total tokens per dollar (serial single-stream floor, no overlap; canonical 25 ms/token basis) | ~199,000 tokens per dollar | 9,500/8.58 ≈ 1,107 tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20; 8.58 s = 1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode at the canonical 25 ms/token rate [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]"
findings.issue: Evidence-label/provenance defect and internal inconsistency: the ~199,000 row is built from the canonical 25 ms/token TPOT and the canonical 1.08 s prefill residual, i.e. from two canonical-scenario inputs, yet it carries [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] because the chapter's 'mixed-input convention' lets the non-canonical ~50 tok/s point govern. But the ~199,000 row itself never uses the 50 tok/s point (it uses the canonical 25 ms/token rate), so the mixed-input convention is being applied to a row with no illustrative input at all. Meanwhile the row immediately above it (~242,000) uses the illustrative 20 ms/token rate and correctly carries [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. The arithmetic itself checks out (9,500/8.58 = 1,107.2 × 3600/20 = 199,300 ≈ 199,000; 9,500/7.08 = 1,342 × 180 = 241,560 ≈ 242,000; 1,583 × 180 = 285,000), so this is a label/provenance mismatch, not a numeric error. Recurrence sweep: the same mixed-input convention is asserted for the whole table on page 131 ('The mixed-input convention therefore governs: the non-canonical input wins, and the rows carry [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] rather than [canonical scenario][DERIVED]') — which mislabels the canonical-input rows.
findings.fix_instruction: Relabel the ~199,000 row [canonical scenario][DERIVED] (its inputs — 9,500 tokens, 8.58 s, 25 ms/token, 1.08 s, $20/hr — are all canonical-scenario values) and restrict the mixed-input convention statement (page 131 note) to the rows that actually consume the ~50 tok/s point (the 9,000 and the ~285,000 rows).

findings.chapter: Ch 5 — From Workload to Model Selection (§5.3(b))
findings.evidence: PDF p.132 (printed p.108): "[1P][FACT]: 8×H100 GPUs provide 8 × 80 GB = 640 GB aggregate HBM memory (real hardware spec)." This contradicts the book's own composite-cell rule (Ch 4, Table 4-2 Note 1: "the 80 GB per GPU is [1P][FACT], the 8-GPU count is [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION], and the 640 GB pool is arithmetic on the two ([1P][FACT] × 8), not a third independent value") and the Preface ("an 8×H100 host — is a scenario choice, not a vendor fact"). The identical quantity is labeled correctly elsewhere: Ch 4 Table 4-1 ("640 GB pool = [1P][FACT] × 8 → [1P][DERIVED] ... the 8-GPU count is a [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] deployment-unit choice, not a vendor fact") and Ch 7 Table 7-1 ("8 ×80 GB = 640 GB ... → [1P][DERIVED]; the 8-GPU host composition is [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]").
findings.issue: Evidence-label/provenance mismatch: the 640 GB aggregate is tagged [1P][FACT] with the gloss "real hardware spec", promoting a scenario deployment-unit composite (scenario 8-GPU count × vendor 80 GB constant) to the strongest first-party label, in direct violation of the book's own composite-cell rule and inconsistent with the labeling of the same quantity in Ch 4 and Ch 7.
findings.fix_instruction: Relabel per Table 4-2 Note 1's composite-cell rule: split the sentence into "80 GB per GPU [1P][FACT] (NVIDIA H100 SXM5 datasheet); the 8-GPU host composition [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]; the 640 GB pool [1P][DERIVED] (that constant × 8)" — or simply cite Ch 4 Table 4-2 — and delete the "(real hardware spec)" gloss as applied to the 640 GB aggregate.
